items.stem:
Read the following billboard advertisement for a smartphone (the image is described in words).

[Image: a vast white space. In the exact centre, a thin black phone stands upright, casting a long soft shadow. Nothing else.]

items.answer: Aphoristic slogan: "Less. But better." – the two short fragments imply quality over quantity and match the minimal design.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why typography matters in an advertisement.

items.stem:
Read the following poster from a multimodal campaign by a youth climate group (the image is described in words).

Analyse how the visual elements of the text contribute to its message.
items.answer: Visual grammar: the drop is the salient central image; the reflected dry riverbed inside it creates a striking visual metaphor linking everyday water use to drought; the pale background and plenty of white space focus attention.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a robot pet, posted on a technology website.

[Image: a silver robot puppy curled on the lap of a smiling elderly man; sunlight through a window.]
MEET PIXEL. HE NEVER NEEDS A WALK. HE NEVER FORGETS YOUR BIRTHDAY.
Powered by AI, Pixel learns your routines, reminds you of medicines and plays your favourite songs.
"I talk to him every morning," says Harold, 81, from Leeds.
Companionship, reinvented. Order today – free delivery.

How does the advertisement present the robot as a comforting companion? Refer to visual grammar (salience, framing, colour, typography, layout).
items.answer: The sunlit image of the puppy on an old man's lap borrows the warmth of a real pet. The anaphora "HE NEVER..." lists advantages, the testimonial from Harold, 81, gives emotional proof, and the slogan "Companionship, reinvented" presents technology as the answer to loneliness. A critical reader may notice that it quietly replaces human contact.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The sunlit image of the puppy on an old man's lap borrows the warmth of a real pet. The anaphora "HE NEVER..." lists advantages, the testimonial from Harold, 81, gives emotional proof, and the slogan "Companionship, reinvented" presents technology as the answer to loneliness. A critical reader may notice that it quietly replaces human contact. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: "Images persuade more than words in advertising." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Images often make the first impact, but words anchor their meaning; effective adverts combine both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: images are processed instantly; they create emotional associations. Arguments against: slogans anchor meaning; words give information and calls to action. Supported judgement: Images often make the first impact, but words anchor their meaning; effective adverts combine both. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Explain why colour choices are important in visual texts.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a candidate for school captain to a Year 10 assembly.

Good morning, Year 10. I'm not going to promise you a swimming pool, a four-day week or free pizza on Fridays. (I asked. The answer was no.)
What I will promise is this: a student council that actually meets, a suggestion box that someone actually opens, and a captain who actually listens.
Last year, ninety of us signed the petition for water fountains on the top floor. Nothing happened. This year, let's make something happen.
Vote Amira. Because "actually" is a promise I can keep.

Describe the tone of the text and explain how the writer creates it.
items.answer: The tone is witty and sincere: self-deprecating humour combined with realistic promises creates a likeable, sincere tone.
items.markingKey: The tone is witty and sincere: self-deprecating humour combined with realistic promises creates a likeable, sincere tone. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Explain the difference between parody and pastiche.
items.answer: Parody imitates in order to mock or criticise; pastiche imitates in a celebratory or neutral way.
items.markingKey: Parody imitates in order to mock or criticise; pastiche imitates in a celebratory or neutral way. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a high-angle shot and a low-angle shot.
items.answer: A low angle looks up at the subject, making it powerful; a high angle looks down, making it vulnerable or small.
items.markingKey: A low angle looks up at the subject, making it powerful; a high angle looks down, making it vulnerable or small. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why advertisers use celebrity endorsement.
items.answer: Audiences transfer their admiration and trust from the celebrity to the product, hoping to share the celebrity's qualities.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Audiences transfer their admiration and trust from the celebrity to the product, hoping to share the celebrity's qualities. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following parody advertisement from a school satirical magazine (the image is described in words).

[Image: a dramatic close-up of a tired student with dark eyes, lit like a perfume model, holding a tiny bottle labelled EXAM. Gold sparkles drift around her. In the background, a pile of textbooks glows like treasure.]
Slogan (elegant gold script): EAU DE EXAM. Because you're worth… a B+.
Small text: The scent of revision, panic and cold toast at 2 a.m. Now with notes of highlighter.
Warning: may cause sudden memories of the periodic table.

Explain how this text borrows the persuasive techniques of a real advert and turns them against advertising.
items.answer: It borrows persuasive techniques (aspirational slogan, glamour, sensory description of "notes") but turns them upside down to make readers laugh at the idea that exam stress is glamorous.
items.markingKey: It borrows persuasive techniques (aspirational slogan, glamour, sensory description of "notes") but turns them upside down to make readers laugh at the idea that exam stress is glamorous. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following magazine advertisement for running shoes (the image is described in words).

[Image: a black-and-white photograph of a young woman running alone up a steep, rain-soaked street at dawn. Only her shoes are in colour – bright orange. She is shot from a low angle, so she appears to tower over the city.]
Slogan (large, white, top left): YOUR ONLY RIVAL IS YESTERDAY.
Small text (bottom right): Olympic 1500 m finalist Zara Kimani trains in Vela Pulse. Built for every kind of morning.
Logo: VELA

Explain how the choice in "Olympic 1500 m finalist Zara Kimani trains in Vela Pulse" contributes to the text's message.
items.answer: Endorsement: "Olympic 1500 m finalist Zara Kimani trains in Vela Pulse" – a respected athlete transfers her credibility to the product.
items.markingKey: Endorsement: "Olympic 1500 m finalist Zara Kimani trains in Vela Pulse" – a respected athlete transfers her credibility to the product. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following poster from a multimodal campaign by a youth climate group (the image is described in words).

[Image: a single drop of water falling from a tap. Inside the drop, reflected upside down, is a cracked, dry riverbed. The background is pale blue, almost white.]
Headline (bold, dark blue): EVERY DROP HAS A HISTORY.
Body text: It takes 2,700 litres of water to make one cotton T-shirt. Before you buy, ask: do I need it?
Call to action: Join the #OneShirtChallenge – wear one T-shirt for a week and post your photo.
Logo: Youth for Water (bottom centre)

How do the visual and verbal elements of the poster work together to persuade? Refer to visual grammar (salience, framing, colour, typography, layout).
items.answer: The salient image of a water drop containing a reflected dry riverbed is a visual metaphor linking everyday water to drought, and the white space keeps the focus on it. The headline "EVERY DROP HAS A HISTORY" invites curiosity, the statistic "2,700 litres" provides logos, and the question "do I need it?" addresses readers personally. The hashtag call to action extends the campaign onto social media, turning viewers into participants.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The salient image of a water drop containing a reflected dry riverbed is a visual metaphor linking everyday water to drought, and the white space keeps the focus on it. The headline "EVERY DROP HAS A HISTORY" invites curiosity, the statistic "2,700 litres" provides logos, and the question "do I need it?" addresses readers personally. The hashtag call to action extends the campaign onto social media, turning viewers into participants. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student council president to her school assembly in Toronto.

Good morning, everyone. Raise your hand if you checked your phone before breakfast today. (Pause.) Me too.
We are the most connected generation in history – and, according to our own school survey, 62 per cent of us say we feel lonely every week. Connected, but alone.
I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake. I'm asking for one hour. One lunchtime a week, phones in our bags, eyes on each other.
Let's try it. Let's talk. Let's remember what our friends' faces look like when they laugh.

Write a response to the speech for the school newspaper (about 200 words), giving your opinion on the phone-free lunchtime idea.
items.answer: Indicative content: headline; clear opinion; reference to the speaker's points (statistic, "Connected, but alone"); one counterargument (e.g. phones help some students feel included); conclusion.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: headline; clear opinion; reference to the speaker's points (statistic, "Connected, but alone"); one counterargument (e.g. phones help some students feel included); conclusion. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).
